title: Paradip Ports & Port Services: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**A Paradip port borrower moves bulk cargo — coal, coke, ore, containers — between rail, road and vessel, and gets paid per tonne handled or per rake unloaded.** Cash comes from port users and traders; the asset base is berths, mechanised handling systems, tipplers, conveyors, barges and trucks. **Value sits in the handling contract and the berth/rail linkage, not in the steel on the ground.** Paradip's own numbers show the volume engine running: daily rake unloading up 15.34% [2] and metallurgical coke handling up 19.54% [3]. Both are local port releases dated late October 2026, so they are current.

## Where cash and value sit
**Pricing power is thin and set by the port tariff and the cargo owner; the operator's margin comes from throughput per shift and equipment uptime.** Capex is heavy and lumpy — a mechanised handling line or a barge is a multi-year commitment — so a borrower's cash is consumed before the first tonne moves. Working capital is the swing item: receivables from traders and steel/cement buyers, plus fuel and spares. **Peer rating work puts a comparable port operator's receivable period at 60 days in FY25 against 52 days in FY24 [8], and another at 57 days in FY23 from 81 days in FY22 [11]** — so when a proposal lands, check the debtor days trend; if receivables are stretching past the peer range, ask which buyer is delaying and whether that buyer is a group company.

## What has changed now
**Volumes are rising but costs are rising with them.** An Emkay note says fuel price adjustments and recovering freight support top-line growth while persistent cost inflation offsets volume expansion in Q2FY27 [7]. Peer results confirm the volume story: Adani Ports reported Q2 FY27 revenue up 23.7% to ₹11,340 crore and Ebitda up 22.6% to ₹6,806 crore at a 60% margin [6], with profit up 16.5% [5]. **That is a large-operator result, not a Paradip SME result — do not read the 60% margin across to a local handling contractor.** Rating reports flag two live risks: service-tax claims on a port group at about 23% of something material [9], and regulatory tightening on coal handling forcing extra capex [11]. Both are dated only by content, so treat them as old until the borrower confirms current status.

## Who to pursue, and how to grow safely
**Pursue mechanised cargo-handling contractors tied to coke and rake-unloading volumes [2][3], barge and lighterage operators with firm charter contracts, and equipment-rental firms serving the berths.** Avoid single-cargo coal handlers with no contract tenure and any borrower whose growth plan is pure capex into coal. Structure as a working-capital line against assigned receivables plus a term loan matched to the handling contract life; take monthly rake/tonnage statements, debtor ageing and a stock-and-equipment statement every month, and a quarterly confirmation of contract renewals. **If the borrower cannot show a contract beyond twelve months, ask for a personal guarantee and a lower drawing limit.**

## Early-warning signs
**Watch tonnage per rake and idle days first — a volume business that stops moving equipment is already in trouble.** Paradip-specific published data is thin beyond the two port releases [2][3]; the local source [1] carries no usable content, so lean on first principles and peer benchmarks. Collect from customer: current receivable days, contract tenure, and cargo mix.
watch: throughput falls below the contracted minimum for two months -> freeze further drawings and reprice
receivable days stretch beyond the peer 60-day level [8] -> ask which buyer and seek assignment of that receivable
tenure under twelve months -> cut limit and add personal guarantee
idle days rise for two consecutive months -> inspect assets and reassess term-loan schedule
borrower confirms tightening rules requiring capex [11] -> require fresh capex plan before any enhancement
